\[
f'(x)=\ln x+1+\frac1x-a.
\]

**(1)** For \(a=1\), \(f(1)=0\) and \(f'(1)=1\). Thus the tangent line is
\[
y=x-1.
\]

**(2)** For \(x>1\),
\[
f(x)>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
a<\frac{x+1}{x-1}\ln x.
\]
The right-hand side is strictly greater than \(2\), because
\[
\ln x-\frac{2(x-1)}{x+1}>0;
\]
indeed, this difference is \(0\) at \(x=1\) and has derivative
\[
\frac{(x-1)^2}{x(x+1)^2}>0\quad(x>1).
\]
Also, \(\frac{x+1}{x-1}\ln x\to2\) as \(x\to1^+\). Hence the condition holds for every \(x>1\) exactly when \(a\le2\).

Final answer: (1) \(y=x-1\); (2) \(a\in(-\infty,2]\).
